system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 16 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2185-10-30 13:10:00 to 2185-11-14 18:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, and multiple prior abdominal surgeries was admitted for acute abdominal pain and projectile vomiting following an abdominal massage. She was recently hospitalized for similar symptoms attributed to pseudoobstruction. On admission, she was in distress with tachycardia and abdominal distension. An NG tube was placed, revealing dilated bowel loops on imaging, but CT scan showed no mechanical obstruction, supporting a diagnosis of pseudoobstruction. She was managed with NPO status, IV fluids, pain control, and serial monitoring. Her renal function improved with hydration, and after two enemas, she passed stool and gradually advanced to a regular diet. The NG tube was repositioned multiple times before being removed. She remained stable, with no medication changes, and was discharged home in good condition able to tolerate oral intake without pain or vomiting.
problems: Dyspepsia and other specified disorders of function of stomach
Other diseases of lung, not elsewhere classified

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ female with multiple small bowel obstructions,
presenting with nausea and vomiting.  Evaluate for small-bowel obstruction.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal radiograph ___ and CT abdomen and pelvis
___.

THREE VIEWS OF THE ABDOMEN:  A nasogastric tube is in place, but the tip
terminates at or just above the gastroesophageal junction and the sidehole is
in the lower esophagus.  The upright view demonstrates no air-fluid levels. 
There is at least one loop of bowel measuring 3.9 cm transverse dimension, but
this may be sigmoid colon left lower quadrant.  Gas is seen in the rectum. 
Note is made of numerous injection granulomas in the buttocks.  Osseous
structures appear unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Nasogastric tube requires advancement. Findings/recommendations posted to
the ED dashboard at 9:20 a.m., ___.

2.  No evidence specific for bowel obstruction.

INDICATION:  ___ female with multiple abdominal surgeries, Crohn's,
with nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain.  Evaluate for obstruction.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen and pelvis, ___, and abdominal radiograph from
earlier the same day.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT helical acquisition was performed from the lung bases through
the pubic symphysis following the uneventful administration of IV contrast. 
Multiplanar reformations were provided.

CT ABDOMEN WITH IV CONTRAST:  The liver, spleen, pancreas, adrenal glands,
left kidney, ureters, and bowel appear unremarkable except for post-surgical
change.  The right kidney demonstrates two subcentimeter hypodensities; likely
cysts.  There is no evidence of bowel obstruction.  Oral contrast has
progressed to the distal ileum.  There is a partial right colonic resection. 
Although no oral contrast has progressed to the left colon, stool and gas is
seen in the sigmoid colon.  There is no abnormally dilated loop of bowel.  The
adrenal glands, kidneys appear normal.  Scattered mesenteric nodes are
prominent, but not pathologically enlarged.  There is no abnormal fluid
collection.

CT PELVIS WITH IV CONTRAST:  The rectum, sigmoid colon, bladder appear
unremarkable.  There is no pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Osseous structures demonstrate normal appearance.

IMPRESSION:   No evidence of small bowel obstruction or other acute process.

MEDICAL HISTORY:  ___ woman with Crohn's disease, multiple episodes of
small bowel obstructions, with extremely difficult IV access.  A request was
placed for either a PICC  or a midline.

CLINICIANS:  Dr. ___, fellow performed the procedure.  Dr. ___
___ the attending radiologist reviewed the study.

ANESTHESIA:  Local anesthesia with 1% lidocaine.

COMPARISON:  Multiple midline PICCs placed previously and previous venograms
showing bilateral central occlusions.

PROCEDURE AND FINDINGS:  The procedure, benefits and risks were explained to
the patient and a verbal consent was obtained.  The patient was placed supine
on the imaging table and the right upper arm was prepped and draped in the
usual sterile fashion.  A pre-procedure  timeout was performed.

Ultrasound examination showed no patent brachial, basilic or cephalic veins.
There was an unnamed venous tributary over the anteromedial aspect of the
upper arm which was suitable for a PICC line placement.  Using sterile
technique and local anesthesia this tributary was punctured under direct
ultrasound guidance using a micropuncture set.  Hard copies of ultrasound
images were obtained before and after establishing intravenous accessand are
on file. A 0.018 guidewire was placed through the needle and the could only be
advanced up to the distal subclavian vein.  A peel-away sheath was placed over
the guidewire and attempts were made to cross the obstruction with a 0.018
Glidewire but were unsuccessful.  A formal venogram was not performed as
patient previously had multiple venograms demonstrating central obstruction
and was also noted to be allergic to iodine-containing contrast media.  A
decision was made to leave a midline rather than a centrally placed PICC line.
A ___ single lumen PICC line catheter measuring 23 cm in length was
placed over the guidewire and advanced into the axillary vein.  The peel-away
sheath and guidewire were then removed.  The catheter was easily aspirated and
flushed.  A fluoroscopic spot film was obtained demonstrating the catheter
position showing the tip terminating in the axillary vein.  The catheter was
secured to skin with a StatLock device and sterile dressings applied.  The
patient tolerated the procedure well and there were no immediate
complications.

IMPRESSION:
Uncomplicated ultrasound and fluoroscopically guided 23-cm midline placement
via an venous tributary access.  Final internal length is 23 cm with the tip
positioned in the axillary vein. The line is ready to use.

MR ENTEROGRAPHY

CLINICAL INDICATION:  ___ woman with history of ___ disease and
worsening nausea, abdominal pain, and low-grade fever.

COMPARISON EXAM:  CT abdomen/pelvis on ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar T1- and T2-weighted MR images were acquired on a 1.5
Tesla magnet including dynamic 3D imaging obtained prior to, during, and after
the uneventful administration of 0.1 mmol/kg of gadolinium-DTPA.  Multiplanar
reformations and subtraction images were generated on an independent
workstation.  1 mg of intramuscular glucagon was administered to restrict
bowel motion.  900 cc of VoLumen was administered orally prior to the
examination.

FINDINGS:

There are multiple prior small bowel and colonic resections. Gastrointestinal
tract is of normal caliber. No abnormal mucosal enhancement, bowel wall
thickening, or surrounding mesenteric inflammatory changes are noted.  No
evidence of fistula or collection. No intra-abdominal ascites.  No significant
lymphadenopathy.

Visualized portion of the liver, spleen, biliary tree, pancreas, and kidneys
are unremarkable.  No abnormal marrow signal is evident.  Mesenteric
vasculature is unremarkable.

Multiplanar 2D and 3D reformations provided multiple perspectives for the
dynamic series.

IMPRESSION:
No MR evidence of active ___ inflammation; no interval changes vs. most
recent prior CT.

Nasogastric tube in place.  Evaluation for placement.

COMPARISON:  ___.

newly inserted.  The tip of the tube is below the diaphragm.  There is no

Normal size of the cardiac silhouette, no pleural effusions, no focal

HISTORY:  ___ female with difficult to assess line placement and

FINDINGS:  Grayscale and Doppler sonograms were performed of the veins of the
right upper extremity.  The right subclavian demonstrates occlusion.  The

IMPRESSION:  Right subclavian thrombosis, age indeterminate.

MEDIAL HISTORY:  ___ woman with Crohn's disease and no IV access.
Patient has history of occlusion of both subclavian veins and has past history
of SVC syndrome.  Patient recently had an ___ placement of right arm
midline which was pulled out because of swelling and right subclavian
thrombus.  A request was placed for a temporary triple-lumen central venous

CLINICIANS:  Dr. ___ and Dr. ___.  Dr. ___ is the
attending radiologist who was present and supervising throughout.

PROCEDURE AND FINDINGS:  An informed written consent was obtained after

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ve been reviewing your case. You came in with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain—can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I’ve had this sharp pain in my right upper abdomen for about four days. It started in my flank and moved up. It comes and goes, but it’s been really bad the last day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And the vomiting—how often have you been vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I vomited once before coming in, but since then it’s mostly dry heaving. I can’t keep anything down. I feel dizzy when I sit up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense—you were dehydrated when you arrived. We’ve already given you fluids and some medication for pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve had these episodes before—usually it’s a bowel obstruction. But this time feels different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan to check for that. Good news—it doesn’t show a mechanical obstruction. Your bowel looks okay structurally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still working that out. Your labs showed a slightly elevated lactate, which was concerning, but it’s coming down. We’re treating you with antibiotics just in case there’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Cipro and Flagyl before. Are you giving me those again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We started those in the ER. We also gave you Dilaudid for pain and Valium to help with the anxiety and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really appreciate the Valium. Being in the hospital brings back bad memories. I get very anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve noted your PTSD history. Psychiatry will be involved to help support your care. We want to make sure you’re as comfortable as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to keep you NPO for now—nothing by mouth—so your gut can rest. We’ll continue IV fluids and monitor your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I’m worried about not eating. With my short bowel, I absorb so little as it is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. That’s why we’re watching your electrolytes and hydration closely. We’ll advance your diet slowly once your symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your abdominal pain is still present, but your vitals are stable. We’re going to try a small amount of ice chips today to see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds okay. I’ve been sipping a little water at home when I feel okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start very slowly. Also, we placed a midline in your right arm yesterday for IV access since your veins are difficult.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I remember. My right arm has been swelling a bit since then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware. We’re going to do an ultrasound today to check for a clot, especially since you have a history of SVC syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound showed a clot in your right subclavian vein. It’s likely related to the midline. We’re going to remove it and place a central line in your neck instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no… is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, but manageable. Because of your history of HIT, we can’t use heparin or Lovenox. We’ll treat you with Fondaparinux instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. But I’m scared of more procedures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll give you Valium beforehand to help with anxiety. The team will go slowly and keep you informed every step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The central line was placed successfully yesterday in your right internal jugular. You’re now on Fondaparinux, and your arm swelling is starting to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt a little better yesterday. Can I try more than ice chips?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can try clear liquids—tea, broth. But we’ll go slow. We also did an MR enterography to check for Crohn’s flare. It showed no active inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a flare? That’s good to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No sign of flare. Your pain seems to be a mix of gastrointestinal discomfort and heightened by anxiety and PTSD. We’re addressing both.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well on clear liquids. We’re going to try advancing to a light diet—soft foods like toast and applesauce.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try, but yesterday when I felt dehydrated, even sipping tea made my pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good observation. Hydration really affects your tolerance. We’ll keep your IV fluids going while you eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool tests came back negative for infections like C. diff, Salmonella, and Campylobacter. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried it was something contagious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your arm swelling is much better. The Fondaparinux is working. We’ll keep you on it until you’re fully improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to take it after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t think so. Since the clot was likely related to the catheter and you have HIT, we’ll stop it once you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re tolerating the soft diet well. We’re going to try regular food today—small portions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but I’m ready to eat real food again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You made it through yesterday’s meals without pain. That’s a big step forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I’m finally turning a corner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry checked in. They agree with continuing Valium every six hours while you’re here. We’ll start a taper when you’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. It really helps me stay calm and reduces the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off IV fluids for 24 hours and still doing well. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been drinking water and eating small meals. I feel stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Potassium was low earlier but is now normal with supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. I take supplements at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days. We’ll write prescriptions for antibiotics to finish at home and a Valium taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I take the Valium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a seven-day taper—start at 4mg every six hours, then gradually reduce to avoid withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing so well. You’ve been walking independently, eating regular meals, and your pain is minimal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really grateful. This stay was scary at first, but I feel safe now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll go home tomorrow. You’ll take Cipro and Flagyl for one more week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have Dilaudid for breakthrough pain and Phenergan for nausea as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my GI and therapist. This experience reminded me how important that is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re ready to go home. Your abdominal pain has resolved, you’re eating well, and your arm swelling is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I know I have a complex history, but you made me feel heard and cared for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Remember the Valium taper—don’t stop it cold turkey. Call us if you have fever, vomiting, or swelling in your arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m ready to rest at home and keep moving forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest and stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m so glad this is behind me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Take it easy and keep in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe journey home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, and multiple prior abdominal surgeries was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Imaging showed no evidence of bowel obstruction or Crohn’s flare, and she was managed supportively with IV fluids, antibiotics, and pain control. She developed right upper extremity swelling related to a midline catheter, and ultrasound confirmed a right subclavian vein thrombosis. Due to her history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, she was treated with Fondaparinux, which resolved the swelling. Her abdominal pain was partially exacerbated by PTSD and anxiety, for which she received Valium with a planned taper. She gradually advanced to a regular diet and was discharged home in stable condition after 15 days, with instructions to complete a 7-day Valium taper, finish a course of antibiotics, and follow up with her outpatient providers.
